articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian 'Oil Trustees' and Issues Cuba FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting four individuals in Iran, identified as 'oil trustees' who facilitate illicit oil sales for the Iranian regime to evade sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade. These individuals are accused of collecting money from international oil sales, often for personal gain, and supporting entities like Mahan Air.

Among those designated are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of the Iranian Football Federation's president. Also sanctioned are Mohammad Hossein Servati, linked to companies brokering Iranian oil shipments to Chinese 'teapot' refineries, and Mojtaba Arabnejad, who allegedly purchased aircraft parts for the sanctioned Mahan Air and oversaw oil sales supporting the airline.

In addition to the Iran designations, OFAC also issued two new Cuba-related Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs 1277 and 1278), providing further guidance on existing Cuba sanctions. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to increase economic pressure on Tehran to address its attacks on Gulf shipping and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and to clarify compliance obligations regarding Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a series of new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. These actions aim to disrupt networks that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing specific authorizations related to certain transactions. This license aims to balance enforcement efforts with humanitarian or other policy considerations.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions. These changes reflect ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions program against Russia, likely in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances and efforts to refine the scope of authorized activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today implemented new counter terrorism designations. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting or engaging in terrorist activities, aiming to disrupt their financial and operational networks.

The designations fall under OFAC's broader mandate to combat global terrorism and protect the U.S. financial system from illicit use. Specific details regarding the designated parties and the nature of their activities were released as part of the announcement.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's continued commitment to using its sanctions authorities to counter the financing and facilitation of terrorism worldwide.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions are part of a concerted effort to combat illicit global networks.

The designations aim to disrupt the financial flows and support structures that enable drug trafficking and terrorist operations. This dual focus highlights the interconnected nature of various illicit activities and the comprehensive approach taken by U.S. sanctions authorities.
Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the reasons for their inclusion on the sanctions list, were provided in the official release.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today published an update to existing Iran designations. This action involves modifications or clarifications to previously announced sanctions against individuals or entities linked to Iran.

Such updates typically involve changes to identifying information, aliases, or other details that enhance the effectiveness of the sanctions program and aid in compliance. The specific nature of the update was detailed in the official announcement.
These ongoing adjustments reflect OFAC's dynamic approach to maintaining and refining its sanctions against the Iranian regime and its illicit activities.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed new Iran-related designations, targeting financial networks that are crucial to sustaining the Iranian regime. These actions are part of an intensified campaign to disrupt Tehran's ability to fund its destabilizing activities.

The sanctions aim to cut off financial channels used by the Iranian government, including those supporting its nuclear program and other malign activities. This move aligns with broader international efforts to pressure Iran into complying with its international obligations.

The designations underscore the U.S. commitment to preventing Iran from accessing sensitive technologies and funding, thereby limiting its capacity for proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities and ballistic missile development.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new sanctions against Cuba. These actions are part of a multi-pronged approach to combat various illicit activities globally.

The Cuba designations include the identification of five vessels as blocked property and the targeting of eight entities and two individuals. OFAC also issued a determination extending Executive Order 14404 to four additional sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine.

Additionally, Chinese military suppliers, China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies Co., Ltd., were designated for materially assisting the Government of Cuba. These companies were accused of supplying equipment to Cuba's military through a Cuban procurement firm.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / World Socialist Web Site

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Amends Venezuela GL, and Issues Alert
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities.

In conjunction with these measures, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, providing guidance and warnings to the public and financial institutions regarding potential risks associated with transactions involving Iran. This alert aims to enhance compliance and prevent sanctions evasion.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This amendment, General License 5AA, further delays the effectiveness of the authorization in GL 5 until December 18, 2026, impacting transactions related to the PdVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This action modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, aiming to refine the scope of permissible activities under the sanctions regime.

General Licenses are frequently updated to address evolving policy considerations, clarify ambiguities, or respond to specific circumstances. The details of this amendment were made available in the official publication.
This amendment is part of OFAC's ongoing management of the Iran sanctions program, which seeks to exert economic pressure while allowing for certain authorized transactions.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Imposes North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting individuals and entities associated with North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These actions aim to address illicit activities in both regions.

The North Korea designations are part of ongoing international efforts to counter Pyongyang's weapons programs and its use of illicit revenue streams. The Democratic Republic of the Congo designations address concerns related to human rights abuses, corruption, or other destabilizing activities in the region.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's commitment to using sanctions to promote stability, human rights, and non-proliferation globally.

articles.headline: EU Expands Russia Sanctions, Targeting Banks, Energy, and Disinformation Networks
body: The European Union has adopted three new legal measures significantly expanding its restrictive measures against Russia, effective November 16, 2026. These actions are a direct response to Russia's ongoing aggression against Ukraine and its destabilizing activities.

The new sanctions introduce parallel listings of 12 individuals and 101 entities under the regime concerning actions undermining Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence. This includes approximately 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, oil and gas companies, refineries, and entities supporting Russia's 'shadow fleet.'

Additionally, the EU expanded its restrictive measures addressing Russia's destabilizing activities, adding 30 individuals and one entity to the sanctions list. These new designations primarily target foreign information manipulation and interference, including the Moscow-based Social Design Agency (SDA), accused of coordinated influence operations against European institutions and public support for Ukraine.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / Morgan Lewis / LILF

articles.headline: UK Updates DPRK Sanctions List, Clarifies Mansudae Overseas Project Group Designation
body: On November 17, 2026, the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List, making a variation to the designation of the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies under The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019.

The update clarifies that the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies, also known as Mansudae Art Studio, has engaged in, facilitated, or been responsible for the exportation of workers from the DPRK to other nations for construction-related activities, including for statues and monuments. These activities generate revenue for the Government of the DPRK or the Workers' Party of Korea.

The company has reportedly conducted business in various countries across Africa and Southeast Asia. The sanctions imposed include asset freezes, prohibitions on chartering ships, closure of representative offices, and prevention of business arrangements.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends DPRK Sanctions List Entry
body: On November 13, 2026, the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1718 (2006) concerning the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) enacted amendments to one entry on its Sanctions List of individuals and entities. The update specifically concerns the Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies.

The amendments, specified with strikethrough and underline in the official entry, clarify details related to the entity. The Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies, also known as Mansudae Art Studio, is designated for its role in exporting DPRK workers to other nations for construction activities, including the creation of statues and monuments, to generate revenue for the DPRK government.

This action by the 1718 Sanctions Committee reflects ongoing international efforts to monitor and enforce sanctions against North Korea, particularly those aimed at disrupting illicit revenue streams supporting its weapons programs.

The specific details of the violations were outlined in OFAC's enforcement release.

This settlement underscores the importance of robust compliance programs for companies operating internationally, particularly concerning U.S. sanctions. Companies are expected to conduct thorough due diligence and implement effective controls to prevent transactions with sanctioned parties or regions.
The penalty serves as a reminder that even inadvertent violations can result in significant financial consequences, and OFAC continues to actively enforce its regulations across various industries.

This substantial penalty highlights the critical importance for financial institutions to maintain comprehensive and effective sanctions compliance programs. Failures in screening, monitoring, or internal controls can lead to significant breaches and severe financial repercussions.

OFAC continues to emphasize that financial institutions are responsible for ensuring that their operations do not facilitate transactions with sanctioned countries, entities, or individuals, and that robust compliance measures are essential to mitigate such risks.

articles.headline: U.S. Treasury Presses Singapore, Malaysia on Iran Sanctions Compliance Amid Strait of Hormuz Closure
body: U.S. Treasury Department officials have met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn them of potential risks if they do not comply with U.S. sanctions on Iran. Washington is urging these countries, as well as law firms and banks operating there, to remain vigilant for Iranian front companies.

This push comes as the U.S. steps up efforts to enforce sanctions in Asia and seeks a swift resolution to the conflict in the Middle East, which has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz for much of this year following U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran.

Both Malaysia and Singapore implement UN Security Council sanctions on Iran. Singapore's government affirmed its commitment to 'doing our part' and 'preventing bad actors from abusing our corporate vehicles,' citing efforts to strengthen vigilance in its maritime and financial industries.

articles.headline: Trump Administration Considers Toppling Cuban Authorities, Intensifies Sanctions
body: The Trump administration is reportedly considering measures to topple Cuban authorities before leaving office, intensifying its campaign of economic pressure against the island nation. President Trump previously signed an executive order declaring Cuba an 'unusual and extraordinary threat' to the U.S. and threatened tariffs on countries supplying it with fuel.

This blockade has led to repeated nationwide blackouts, severe fuel and food shortages, and a humanitarian crisis in Cuba, which Cuban officials have described as 'collective punishment.' Washington has progressively added sanctions, targeting Cuba's state oil company, President Miguel Diaz-Canel, and relatives of former President Raul Castro.

A new round of sanctions was announced this month, targeting ten individuals and entities tied to the Cuban government, military, and oil industry. Additionally, a U.S. arrest warrant has been issued for Raul Castro.

These approvals have unlocked over €33 billion in combined public and private investment, aiming to strengthen and diversify Europe's position across the semiconductor value chain.

These investments cover a wide range of semiconductor activities, from wafers and chips to advanced packaging, testing and assembly, and from highly specialized materials to power electronics. Each project is designed to bring additional capacity and innovation to the European semiconductor ecosystem, thereby reducing strategic dependencies.

The European Chips Act, which outlines three pillars of action to reinforce the semiconductor ecosystem in the EU, focuses on security of supply and resilience in its second pillar. These decisions, concerning investments across the EU, are expected to boost wider economic activity and advance the EU's technological sovereignty goals.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
